en: The *Xuánjiàn wǔzōng* (The Five Houses Reflected in the Mysterious Mirror) cites the direct pointing and single transmission that is fundamentally free from artifice. Who would dare to proclaim the subtle mystery that the five houses do not transmit?
Later, as the Dharma grew old and fell into decline, heterodoxies arose; thus, those who followed the gates and side-doors of the five houses sometimes established [their own] five [houses].

The positions of ruler and subject are established; there are four kinds of discernment, three gates, and nine threads. The ten wisdoms accord with reality, and the various schools stand as distinct gateways, each proclaiming its own teaching.
Although these were established for a single period, who knows that the descendants of later generations have fallen one by one into the towering thorns of the forest?
Branches entangle branches and vines lead to more vines; I, this mountain hermit, am ashamed of my inability to pull them out.

With a single sound from the ground, he became a loyal minister to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, utterly incinerating all conceptual molds. Now, you instead take these seven hundred years of stale, rotten vines and re-spin them once more;
this is like painting legs on a snake—before those with clear eyes, you cannot escape being seen as a ghost in broad daylight.
In the second month of winter in the Dingwei year of the Wanli era, the junior monk Juexu of Shaoshi Mountain recognized the profound mirror of the Chan school.

As for those who follow the traces of the sages, they serve as temporary lodgings for former saints and as mirrors for later generations; if one is ignorant of their source, how can one [attain realization]?
This is truly capable of illuminating the Great Matter. I fear that later students might confuse gold with sand or view jade as being the same as stone;
thus, they would become lost in the discourse on guest and host and fail to investigate the principles of honor and subordination.

For this reason, I have gathered the profound mysteries of the ancient sages' mechanisms and synthesized their essential points into twelve gates. Following the currents and arranging the branches, each has its own destination, beginning from the shallow...

Furthermore, as these [teachings] are profoundly unified without divergence, they are titled *The Diagram of the Mysterious Mirror*. It is hoped that those with the discerning eye of the Dharma will examine and verify them in detail.
I have briefly indicated the general direction according to their respective categories; the rest may be understood accordingly.
The Gate of Samantabhadra is like Ruiyan calling out and responding to himself; Dayang performing a dance; Touzi standing up; Zhaozhou patting his knee; National Teacher An winking;
Niaochao blowing on his cloth; Master Mao spreading his two hands; and the essence and function of the Three Mysteries.
All of these belong to the gate of conforming to principle (*yulimen*).
As for the Gate of Mañjuśrī, Mingjue said: "The cold hues of a thousand peaks; raindrops fall upon mountain flowers. Master Yi said: "Vivid greenness on the crags..."
Lowering the bamboo pole: "The lush pines by the mountain stream. An ancient worthy said: "From where does the wind come? What color is the rain?
If someone were to ask this, it refers to all things before one's eyes—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
Guanyin’s Gate is like National Teacher Fuzhang clapping his hands, Mingjue knocking on his meditation seat, Yaoshan beating the drum, and Guishan striking the wooden fish;
it is like Puhua shaking his bell by the ear, Xuansha striking the brazier with a fire-tongs, and even hitting the cauldron to question the monks.
It is so. Because the principle follows the gate, as it is said, "The National Teacher runs and runs; the pillar drags the ox into your nostrils. Touzi—
Yun-liao-jue said, "A girl with horns and a white-haired grandson. Xuan-sha said, "The winter cold is at its peak; the Southern Star suppresses the Northern Dipper;
red dust arises from the bottom of the sea; white waves surge from the mountain peaks," and so forth. These are all like this.
To accord with reality, one relies on the five gates, as Mingjue said:
"The eyes look at green water; the back leans against the green mountains. Shitou said: "The eyes see forms; the ears hear sounds. Nanquan said:
"If you ask about water, I answer with water; if you ask about insects, I answer with insects. By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars," and so forth.
This must truly be profound; it is the fundamental portion. It is not yet permissible to fail to see the principle mentioned above.
Regarding the "Gate of the Natural Body of Dharma," as Mingjue said:
"The sun rises at the edge of heaven, the moon descends. Yunmen said: "Clouds rise on the southern mountain, [the rain falls on the northern mountain]."
It rains. Fish in the depths of the water, birds in the heavens above. Bamboo in the southern lands, wood in the northern lands.
Fire is warm, wind is cool, earth is solid, and water is moist—such are these things. They cannot be expressed through boastful words, nor can they be grasped by the conceptualizing mind.
The "Secret Response" (Miying) is the Gate of Concealing the Point (Zangfengmen).
As Mingjue looked left and right, he called out, "Ancestor, come here to wash your hands. He struck the meditation platform and said, "A phantom has appeared.
Suddenly picking up his staff, he descended from the seat. Zihu shouted at a monk, saying, "Look at the dog! Daci asked Zhaozhou about Prajñā’s rebuke.
This refers to such acts as laughing loudly and Puhua kicking over the rice table.
Regarding the correspondence between phenomena and principle, Mingjue said:
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Did you personally see Nanquan? He replied, "In Zhenzhou, they produce large..."
"Radish. Baoling said, "When the chicken is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it goes down into the water.
This is the same as the case in the previous section; they are all skillful means used to deceive people.
Entrusting matters to signify the profound gate, as Xuefeng answered Tanzhuan: "Within it is gold sufficient to fill a nation.
Yunmen said: "The staff transforms into a dragon. Baling said: "Coral branches support the moon branch by branch. Huangbo said: "The Great Tang..."
Wumen Heshang and others were like this. Because they had exhausted the Dharma and did not wish to speak of it further, they entrusted the matter to these accounts.
As Mingjue said: "Do not say that because the water is cold the fish do not eat; now I have caught them until my boat is full."
The *Lijuequanshi men* (Gate of the Principle that Transcends Verbalization) states:

"Zen practitioners who carry a single board are as numerous as hemp and millet. This refers, for example, to the case where an outsider asked the Buddha whether he would speak of existence or non-existence, and the Tathāgata remained silent for a long while.

The Gate of Following Cessation to Return to Reality is like Baizhang hanging his whisk back in its original place; it is like the monk pushing over the meditation seat and departing; it is like Xuefeng throwing down his whisk;
it is like Yuanming leaning against his staff; and it is like the man from Mingzhou carrying his sack on his back.
The ten gates above all serve to bring this back to one's own fundamental share.
The gate of the total functioning and the exhaustive dharma:
whatever has a point of reference is not the total functioning; even if there is but a single path, nothing is let pass. None of them...

The exhaustion of dharmas is like Great Compassion returning to the abbot’s quarters; it is like Mingjue ordering Nanquan to strike Zhaozhou and then drive him out, or like facing all eight directions and four quarters, properly striking back blow for blow.
Furthermore, there were three catties of remaining hemp; nine times nine is eighty-one.
There is the story of how a single cotton shirt made in Qingzhou weighs seven and a half catties. This has always been without support and transcends all measurement; therefore, it is not grasped.
Moreover, there are further expedient means such as direct pointing and secret pointing, as clarified within the Three Mysteries and Eight Potencies. If you wish to know them, examine the diagrams.
Gather what you have received back to its source; when the principles and patterns are examined in detail, clear awakening should become visible.
Furthermore, regarding the three grades of the gate:
if one enters through the Gate of Avalokiteśvara, even all frogs and earthworms will assist you in triggering the initial movement of the mind.
If you enter through the gate of Mañjuśrī, even walls, fences, tiles, and rubble will assist you in triggering your awakening.
If you enter through the gate of Samantabhadra, every lifting of a foot, every movement of a step, and every application of effort will be such as to assist you in triggering your awakening.

In the Hall of the Elder Yanming, the author of the *Sanxuan Lun*, he questioned National Teacher Tiantai Shaoguo, saying: "What is the general meaning of the discourse and dialogues presented in the School of the Patriarchs?
The National Teacher replied: "The general meaning does not go beyond the Three Mysteries. He asked: "What are called the Three Mysteries?"

The National Teacher said: "First is the mystery of reality (shixuan); second is the mystery of essence (tixuan); third is the mystery of function (yongxuan). A question was asked: "What is meant by the mystery of reality?

The National Teacher said: "Generally speaking, when questions and answers do not exceed what ordinary people discuss, and all accord with matters of one's own fundamental allotment, this is called the mystery of reality.
For example, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, 'What is Zhaozhou? he replied:"
He said, "The East Gate, the West Gate, the South Gate, and the North Gate. When asked, "What is the Master of Zhaozhou?
he replied, "It is the Great King. Furthermore, it is like when Nanquan was walking with several monks and saw the water in a pond.
Also, it is like when Elder Yukui asked Fayan, "What is the True Dharma Eye? and he replied, "That which sees form right now is it."
Furthermore, it is like striking the ground with a ball, pointing toward the heavens, or blowing on a tuft of cloth; responding in accordance with the actual reality of whatever the student asks.

According to this principle, one does not reveal one's sharp edges, does not deviate from ordinary discourse, and does not lose the functional pivot—all of these are matters of one’s own fundamental allotment (*bun-bun*).
From antiquity to the present, that which constitutes the fundamental and true mystery is precisely the ultimate point of the Zen school.
This is the method for examining it. Question: What is meant by "the Real" (shí)? Answer: It cannot be understood through conceptual assembly nor investigated through logical deduction;
because it is nameless, it is called "the Real. Question: What is meant by "the Mysterious" (xuán)? Answer: Vivid and numinous, its fundamental nature is just so;
therefore, it is called "the Mysterious. Question: What is meant by "one's own original portion" (běnfèn)? Answer: It is that.
Phenomena are not devoid of even a single thing, nor do they transcend the speech, conversation, conduct, and actions of ordinary people;
therefore, these constitute one's fundamental duty (*bun-bun*). Question: What is called "not one's fundamental duty"? Answer:

To speak of performing wondrous enlightenment, bodhi, buddha-nature, knowledge and vision, or the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages—this is to have, within a mind that has nothing to be attained, a semblance of something existing.
Those who claim that there is neither name nor mind, and that nothing can be attained, are all said to lack the fundamental portion [of the teaching]. Question:

What is meant by "the essence is profound" (tǐ xuán)? Answer: As for the essence being profound, it refers to the manifestation of the true essence of the great lunar disc by the Western Heaven patriarch Nāgārjuna.
It is also the primordial, eternal, and true nature inherent in all sentient beings.
The Way is also the ultimate principle discussed in the Great Canon, and it is likewise the forked path where the ancients engaged with students.

It is, for instance, like the ancients of antiquity who brandished their mallets, raised their fly-whisks, pointed their fingers, rolled balls, called out to themselves and answered themselves, or employed the method of the lion entering its den.
That which is profoundly remote and where all traces of the self are severed—these all manifest this fundamental substance. Question:

Since it is the true, substantial nature of the Great Moon-Disk of True Suchness (*tathatā*), why did the ancients speak of "breaking it down into mud and water," and call such a person one who "plays with the spirit and pursues a hollow livelihood"?
Answer: It is because they do not recognize the matter of the supreme, fundamental portion; they merely...
To recognize superficial appearances is called "extreme adherence," and it is for this reason that they are refuted. Question: What is meant by "employing the profound" (*yong xuan*)? Answer:
Employing the profound refers to the ultimate function inherent within the substance of the Great Moon-Disk (*mahā-candramaṇḍala*).
Since ancient times, all masters have employed this method to guide sentient beings. For example, Shenhui shook his body; Daguang performed a dance; and Puhua gazed into the distance.
"True. From east to west, the lion emerges from its cave with no place to hide; all of this manifests this great function. He asked:

"If it is indeed the inconceivable and ultimate function, why did the ancients break it down as being like rubble, or as something turned by the power of a wild fox spirit, such that none of it possesses true reality? He answered: "It is because they do not recognize the direction [of its operation]."

The aforementioned concerns the fundamental reality; yet people merely dally with superficial appearances, clinging to the heterodox as the authentic. It is in this manner that they are refuted. Question:
Why did the ancients refuse to speak of the truth directly, instead requiring the use of the striking of the mallet and the raising of the whisk to provide indirect instruction?

Answer: Explanations based on names and forms lead to many points of stagnation and confusion. There is a fear that they might mislead later students and result in fragmented understanding. Alas!... [text ends]
This is why it is so after having attained [realization]. Question: Among the ancients, there were those who wept and those who laughed; what does this mean? Answer:
Those who laugh receive many rewards, while those who weep receive many punishments. Rewards and punishments are not fixed. Question:

As for the aforementioned Three Mysteries (Sanxuan), is that all, or is there something else distinct from these three mysteries? Answer: Beyond this, there are further Three Essentials (Sanyao). Question: What are they?
What are called the three essentials? First, illumination followed by function; second, function followed by illumination;
third, simultaneous illumination and function.
Now, regarding the first—illumination followed by function—when a student comes, the master of Chan first asks from where [he has come].
"From where have you come? Or, [the master] might ask, "What words or phrases did that teacher use to instruct you?

When the student offers various words and phrases, the Chan master counters by asking, "How do you understand this? Based on this precedent, the ancients also provisionally named this "The Essential Illumination."
Second, regarding "first using [the means] and later illuminating [the truth]": for example, when a student comes to ask about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West,
or asks about the general purport of the Buddha-dharma, or asks what the student’s original face is,
or asks what the ultimate matter is, the Master of Chan may raise his whisk, or take up his staff and strike them, or simply give a shout.
Standing upon the meditation seat, he may draw a circle, or manifest a pivotal point of the teaching; according to these methods, he receives the student.
This is what the ancients also termed "the application of the essential.
Third, regarding "illumination and function occurring simultaneously": for example, when a student comes to pose a question, the master of Chan may [raise his staff] vertically.
He raises his whisk and says, "Is there such a thing as this in any quarter? Or he points to the empty space and asks, "Do you understand?
When a student sees him raise the whisk, they immediately prostrate; the Chan master then says, "This dull-witted fellow. Or the student says, "I do not understand.
The Chan master then points to a pillar and asks, "Does this one understand? The student may then unfold their sitting mat.

Or, raising his fist and palm, the Master said, "This fellow who dabbles with spirits. Judging by this engagement of the pivot, one might say that even the ancients were merely giving a forced name to what is simultaneously illumination and function; yet it is essential.
The Inquiry on the Four Great Models asks:
Beyond the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials, what further teachings are shown to disciples? The answer is: there are the Four Great Models.
The first is the Great Rite of Right Benefit, such as when the First Patriarch was at Shaolin and other instances.
The second is the Great Rite of Equality, such as when Heyuan struck the drum.
The third is the Great Formula of the True and the False, which generally encompasses the two preceding formulas.
The fourth is the Great Formula of the Fundamental Division, such as when the First Patriarch said, "I do not know," upon meeting Emperor Wu of Liang.

The *Bānglùn* (Treatise on the Eight Blows) asks: "Is this it alone, or is there something else? The answer says: "Within the entire lineage of the School of the Patriarchs, there are furthermore several types of precedents.
I shall briefly outline their general features for you. For instance, there is the blow used when drawing out a pivot or delivering a 'hanging word' (*chuyǔ*)."
Briefly, there are eight kinds. The question is asked: What are called the "Eight Sticks"?
First is the Stick of Touching the Profound Branches: tonight, no answers to questions will be given; anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows.
At that time, a monk came forward to prostrate, and the Master struck him—this is it.
The second instance of meeting a visitor with a staff from the outset is as follows: When a monk was struck, he asked, "Why did you strike me before I had even asked?
The Master said, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am from Silla. The Master said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, you deserve thirty blows."
The third is the "Correct Staff for Discerning the Mechanism," as when the Elder Paramārtha’s deportment was not solemn and his ritual etiquette was negligent;
the Master of Chan then struck him—this is it.
The fourth is the "Correct Staff for Relying on the Profound to Wound the Right," as when Dàchánfó arrived at Yǎngshān and stood on one foot, saying, "The West..."
The twenty-eight patriarchs of the heavens were likewise so; the six patriarchs of the Tang land were likewise so; the Master was likewise so;
and I [Somakha] was likewise so—this is the case with Yangshan’s four blows.

The fifth is the "Staff of Following the True Vehicle" (Yinshun Zongsheng Bang). This refers to when a master of Chan and a student engage in a dialogue with profound mutual resonance, and the master then strikes him—this is it.

The sixth is the "Staff of Blind Branding and Sightless Forging" (Mangjia Xialian Bang). This refers to when an elder monk wields his staff while a student cries out, "Strike! Strike! (Chubang Chubang).
The Master has no further response; this is it.
The seventh is the "Staff for Examining Reality and Falsity. For example, when the Chan Master poses a counter-question and the student reaches the ultimate point in their answer.
It is precisely when the Chan master strikes that he is correct.

Furthermore, it is like the staff used to sternly rebuke ignorance: when a student comes to seek instruction and the Elder provides various kinds of guidance, yet the student fails to understand anything at all, it is precisely then that the Elder strikes.
Furthermore, it is like Xuefeng carrying a bundle of rattan on his back; when he encountered a monk on the road, he threw it down.
Just as the monk was about to pick it up, Xuefeng kicked him over. This is it.
The eighth is the staff that sweeps away both the ordinary and the sage. Whether one has attained the Way or not, one strikes.
This alone is the true staff. *Wujulun*.

It is like when a monk asked Zhaozhou: "Leaving behind the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I ask the Master to point directly to the meaning of that man from the West.
The Master said: "This old monk is so dead that he is in haste. This is it.

it does not depend on artificial establishment, nor has it ever increased or decreased. Shitou ceased his preaching, Baizhang rolled up his mat, and Mazu descended from the seat—all these manifested the original state.
